title: British Colonial Empire
capsule: Framed across nearly three centuries, the 'British Colonial Empire' spans from the 1707 Acts of Union that created a unified British state able to project naval and commercial power, through eighteenth-century rivalry with France and the Netherlands for Atlantic and Indian Ocean territory, to the nineteenth-century zenith of Pax Britannica underpinned by Royal Navy supremacy and formal Dominion status for settler colonies such as Canada and Australia. Two world wars drained the metropole's capacity to hold the empire together, and a rapid wave of decolonization from the 1940s through the 1980s dismantled Crown rule across Asia, Africa, and the Caribbean. The arc closes symbolically with the 1997 handover of Hong Kong, the 2000 endpoint here reflecting the empire's final residue of dependent territories still administered from London.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Territorial boundaries of British colonial possessions in this period are well documented through Admiralty charts, Colonial Office records, and treaty texts; internal frontier zones in West Africa and parts of Central Asia are approximate, but core territories are precisely attested.
